title: Potatoes: calories, fiber, potassium, and nutrition

seo.title: Potatoes: calories, fiber, potassium, and nutrition
seo.meta_description: Raw potato provides about 77 kcal, 17.5 g carbs, 2.2 g fiber and 425 mg potassium per 100 g. Cooking method can change the final calorie density.
seo.search_intent: Understand potato calories, fiber, potassium, and how preparation changes the nutrition profile.

excerpt: Potatoes are relatively low in calories when cooked without much added fat. Per 100 g raw, they provide about 77 kcal, 17.5 g carbohydrate, 2.2 g fiber, 2 g protein and roughly 425 mg potassium; frying changes the picture mainly because the potato absorbs oil.
content_html:
Potatoes are often described in two completely different ways: either as a simple, light staple or as a high-calorie food. The potato itself explains only part of that contrast. Cooking method and added fat explain much of the rest.

What 100 g of potato provides

As a practical reference, 100 g of raw potato with skin provides about 77 kcal, 17.5 g carbohydrate, 2 g protein, 2.2 g fiber and 425 mg potassium. Its natural fat content is close to zero.

Most of its calories therefore come from starch. Potato is not a high-protein or high-fat food, but it does make a meaningful contribution of potassium and a modest amount of fiber, especially when the edible skin is included.

Cooking changes concentration

Boiling can change water content and can move some water-soluble minerals into the cooking water. Boiled potato is roughly 87 kcal and 20 g carbohydrate per 100 g, compared with about 77 kcal and 17.5 g in raw potato. The per-100-g shift is largely about water and concentration rather than starch suddenly appearing.

The bigger change comes from added oil. Boiled or baked potato with little added fat generally stays around 80–100 kcal per 100 g, while French fries can easily exceed 300 kcal per 100 g because oil becomes part of the food during frying.

Potassium is one of potato's strengths

At about 425 mg potassium per 100 g raw, potato is a useful source of this mineral. A 200 g portion would provide roughly 850 mg before allowing for cooking losses.

Potassium is involved in nerve signaling, muscle function and fluid balance. Boiling in a large volume of water can reduce the amount retained in the potato because some potassium leaches into the water.

How much fiber does potato contain?

Raw potato with skin provides about 2.2 g fiber per 100 g, or roughly 4.4 g in a 200 g portion. The skin contributes, but it is not the only source of fiber; the flesh contains fiber too.

Potato can help add fiber to a meal, but cooked legumes are much more concentrated sources: many provide about 6–8 g fiber per 100 g, compared with roughly 2 g in potato.

Does potato itself cause weight gain?

A plain 200 g cooked potato may provide around 170 kcal. If 200 g of fried potato reaches about 300 kcal per 100 g, that same weight can approach 600 kcal. The difference is driven mainly by absorbed oil, not by a dramatic change in the potato's original starch.

The useful takeaway

Potato is mainly a carbohydrate food, with plenty of potassium and modest amounts of fiber and protein. If you want its nutrition without greatly increasing calorie density, boiling, steaming, microwaving or baking with little added fat produces a very different result from deep-frying.

faq.question: How many calories are in 100 g of potato?
faq.answer: Raw potato is about 77 kcal per 100 g. Cooked with little added fat, it is commonly around 80–100 kcal per 100 g, while fried potato can exceed 300 kcal per 100 g.

faq.question: Are potatoes high in potassium?
faq.answer: They are a useful source. Raw potato provides about 425 mg potassium per 100 g, although boiling in plenty of water can reduce the amount retained.

faq.question: Is it better to eat potato skin?
faq.answer: The skin adds fiber and some micronutrients. It can be eaten when the potato is well washed, sound and free from problematic green areas or sprouts.
